units.en: A ship refers both to a piece of ⟦0⟧ produced by ⟦1⟧ and, once launched and manned, a member of a ⟦2⟧ ready to participate in ⟦3⟧.

Hulls are the foundational component of ships and are unlocked through ⟦0⟧. Each hull type contains a number of ⟦1⟧ with restrictions and limitations based on the specific hull type. These slots can be populated by ⟦2⟧ via the ⟦3⟧ in order to form complete ship designs that can be produced by ⟦4⟧.
At the start of the game, each country will have a selection of ⟦0⟧ available for production, based upon hull types which have already been researched.

Some hull types may serve as the foundation for more than one ship type, depending upon the modules that are fitted during the design of a given ship variant. For example, ⟦0⟧ can serve as the basis for light cruisers or heavy cruisers depending upon the type of guns that are fitted.
Hull types and their corresponding ship type(s) are listed below:
Panzerschiff hull Coastal Defense Ship hull

Surface warships are categorized either as ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧, while submarines and convoys have their own unique mechanics.
As the main surface combatants, capital ships are designed to sink enemy ships in surface battles.

⟦0⟧ (BB): With their heavy armor, battleships are capable of surviving substantial amounts of incoming fire from the enemy battle line. They can also deal considerable damage of their own. Battleships are expensive and take some time to build.

⟦0⟧ (BC): Battlecruisers share the same hull as battleships and use the same types of armament, but are distinguished by somewhat lighter armor and a lower construction cost. Although they can withstand less damage than a battleship, their lighter weight also makes them faster and slightly harder to hit.

⟦0⟧ (SHBB): SHBBs are particularly powerful and heavily-armored battleships based upon a dedicated SHBB hull, though they are referred to as BBs in-game. Unlike other hulls which receive new iterations over the years, there is only one SHBB hull in the tech tree. SHBBs are powerful enough to remain a potent threat throughout the game despite the lack of hull iterations. However, they are also prohibitively expensive and take a very long time to build.

⟦0⟧ (CA): Heavy cruisers share the same hull as light cruisers, and are distinguished by their heavier guns. With the lightest armor of any capital ship, heavy cruisers have low survivability against battlecruisers and battleships.

⟦0⟧ (CB): Large cruisers are specialized heavy cruisers that are built using more expensive Panzerschiff and Coastal Defense Ship hulls, though they are still referred to as CAs in-game. They can mount even heavier guns that match those found on battleships and battlecruisers. However, despite having costs comparable to battlecruisers, they are similarly lightly armored as regular heavy cruisers and so are no less survivable.

⟦0⟧ (CV): Dedicated aircraft carriers can carry deploy specialized carrier air wings for various tasks, including vying for control of the air and dealing bomb damage to enemy ships during ⟦1⟧, as well as being deployed on ⟦2⟧ outside of them. They can be expensive to build and to fuel, especially with their accompanying aircraft, but can be highly effective for their cost.

⟦0⟧ (CVE): Smaller and cheaper aircraft carriers with only one or two hangar slots, these designs are made possible with the ship designer, though they are still referred to as CVs in-game. While they can be built out of the same hulls as dedicated carriers, they can also be converted from cruisers, which can be a way to keep a navy's aging cruisers relevant for longer. Slow and unable to field as many air wings, they are less effective in battle, but because they can be produced in much larger numbers, they can be deployed in a much wider capacity.
⟦0⟧ are named for their ability to protect capital ships and convoys from torpedoes during naval battles.

⟦0⟧ (CL): Tougher and more expensive than destroyers, light cruisers are highly versatile and can be outfitted for a range of roles. When equipped with airplane catapults, they can serve as excellent scouts. When dedicated to firepower, they excel at destroying other screens and can even put a dent into more lightly armored, enemy heavy cruisers.

⟦0⟧ (DD): As the lightest screen ships, the strength of destroyers lies in their numbers. During battle, they can form the bulk of a screening line to protect capital ships from torpedoes. Destroyers are also ideally suited to convoy escort missions. Both of these roles call for a sufficient quantity of ships, and destroyers are the most economical vessel to produce in the numbers required. They also boast relatively low fuel requirements. Beyond their basic armament, they can be outfitted with additional guns to increase their effectiveness against other screen ships, or torpedoes to threaten capital ships. Further reading: ⟦1⟧.
List of 1936 start legacy deployed destroyers

⟦0⟧ (SS): Cheap, slow, and stealthy, submarines are frequently used as convoy raiders and minelayers. During ⟦1⟧, submarines may be ⟦2⟧ under certain circumstances, which protects them from attack, and even when they are revealed, they can only be damaged by other ships using depth charges. They are, however, particularly vulnerable to patrolling aircraft, especially outside of battles.

⟦0⟧ (SSN): Nuclear submarines are special submarines available with ⟦1⟧ that run on nuclear power instead of combustion engines. As such, they consume no fuel and have a very long operational range, though they are more easily spotted than more advanced non-nuclear submarines and require a lot of technological development to produce.

⟦0⟧ (SSB): Missile launching submarines, also known as ballistic missile submarines, are submarines available with ⟦1⟧ that are equipped with missile-launching bays. They can therefore be used as mobile launch platforms for ⟦2⟧ for a variety of tasks. However, they also require a lot of technological development.

⟦0⟧ (SSBN): Nuclear missile launching submarines, also known as nuclear ballistic missile submarines, are a combination of nuclear submarines and ballistic missile submarines available with ⟦1⟧. Being able to launch a variety of ⟦2⟧ silently from anywhere in the world is a very potent combination, albeit one that requires inordinate amounts of technological investment.
⟦0⟧ are ships which carry land units, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, reinforcements, and ⟦3⟧ equipment across water. They are treated more abstractly than all other ship types, with a variety of unique mechanics.
Convoys are distinguished by the following characteristics:
⟦0⟧ are mostly unarmed, except for 0.25 Light Gun with Piercing 1 and 0.1 Anti-Air.⟦1⟧

The positions of convoys are not shown on the map, regardless of map mode. (Convoy ⟦0⟧ can be seen on the ⟦1⟧.) Convoys are only ever directly seen during naval battles, e.g. when a ⟦2⟧ task force automatically interdicts some convoys.

Damaged convoys do not need to return to dockyards in order to be repaired. Any convoy that is damaged (but not destroyed) during battle will be immediately restored to perfect condition after the battle has ended.
Convoys that are not currently in use are kept in an abstract reserve, and have no tangible presence in the game world.
Convoys cannot be directly controlled by the player. However, it is possible to influence convoy routes by setting ⟦0⟧ for specific regions.
The concepts of hulls and modules do not apply to convoys. Instead, there is only one standard convoy model. There are no technologies available to unlock more advanced convoy models.
It is not possible to create convoy variants or designs.
Convoys can be ⟦0⟧ to other countries and are the only ships that can be transfered in this way (outside of ⟦1⟧ and unique ⟦2⟧).
Convoys are defenseless against enemy warships, but can be ⟦0⟧ by friendly warships for protection.

Left clicking on a ship silhouette in the fleet will bring up its ship details. From here its ⟦0⟧ are visible, along with any combat history on the second tab. It is possible to ⟦1⟧ the ship by pressing its name. Carriers will show the attached air wings. Reorganizing air wings is done through the ⟦2⟧ management system. To ⟦3⟧ a ship, press the red trash bin in the upper right corner of the ship detail screen, this will return its ⟦4⟧ to the pool and is an alternative to sending old ships off on suicidal missions.

When building a carrier, the player has the option to pre-define how its air wings should be organized. Only carrier-capable aircraft may be based on carriers, and must be produced and either researched or designed (depending on whether ⟦0⟧ is active or not) separately from their land-based counterparts. The air wings of existing carriers can be adjusted by selecting the air wing in the air force overview or by selecting an air region in the air map mode, which brings up a list of all bases, and then selecting the fleet the carrier is a part of to bring up the air base windows for all carriers in that fleet. From the (carrier) base window, the process is identical to establishing or managing a wing stationed at an air base.

Hearts of Iron IV tracks the ⟦0⟧, skill, and history of individual ships, which can be seen in the Fleet View. Select the fleet which the player wants to review. You will notice that each individual ship in your fleet is listed with a green organization and a brown strength bar, a silhouette for the ship class, a rank icon to show the ship's experience level, a vertical progress bar showing how much experience that ship has accumulated towards the next rank and the name of the ship. If the ship has participated in combat and sunk any enemy vessels, an additional icon appears next to the ship name for history. Holding the mouse over this history icon will give you a summary of how many ships the player has sunk with this vessel. Clicking on the history icon will open the ship details pop up displaying the history of ships sunk for that particular vessel.

Each class of ship has a number of values referred to as stats. These are described below. Most of these stats can be improved by building a new ⟦0⟧. Researching ⟦1⟧ can also increase certain stats, as can employing the right ⟦2⟧ and, with ⟦3⟧, using ⟦4⟧ spirits. Some ⟦5⟧ can also provide ⟦6⟧ that affect certain ship stats.

⟦0⟧ Maximum speed represents a value that indicates how quickly a naval vessel can move under optimal conditions. A faster ship has an easier time of disengaging from pursuers. It is also less likely to be hit by enemy fire, can pursue contacts easier when spotting the enemy, can evade enemy patrols for longer, and moves faster outside of battle.
⟦0⟧ A ship's range represents its onboard stores of fuel and foodstuffs, which will limit how far it can travel from the nearest friendly ⟦1⟧

⟦0⟧ Organization is an indicator of a ship's combat readiness. The higher the organization rating of a ship, the longer it can stay in a fight. A ship with low or no organization cannot fight or move effectively. See also ⟦1⟧.

⟦0⟧ Deck size is a measurement of how many planes a carrier can fit on board. The act of exceeding a carrier's deck size (plane limit) is known as ⟦1⟧ and it results in a penalty to carrier plane missions. See also ⟦2⟧.
⟦0⟧ HP is an abbreviation for "hit points" and is the ability to absorb damage. It represents strength which is how much damage a ship can sustain before being destroyed.

⟦0⟧ Reliability is the ability of a ship to continue functioning during combat. The lower the value the more likely the ship is of suffering a critical hit. Ships may receive critical hits that are much stronger than usual hits primarily because of exploding ammo or fuel tanks. Increasing a ship's reliability will reduce the chance that a received hit becomes critical. Note that the highest critical chance is done by torpedoes and not by a ship's main guns. Reference ⟦1⟧.
⟦0⟧ How much supply the unit consumes per day. Please read ⟦1⟧ on the significance of this.
⟦0⟧ Damage done by light guns. Light guns are better at targeting smaller ships, but can only target the first non-empty row in ⟦1⟧.
⟦0⟧ Damage done by the heavy guns. Heavy guns are better at targeting bigger ships and can target the first two non-empty rows in ⟦1⟧.
⟦0⟧ Torpedo attack is a value that represents a vessel's capability to damage enemy ships via torpedoes. Torpedoes can target any row in ⟦1⟧, but can be blocked by ⟦2⟧.
